reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Agentic RAG: Retrieval That Can Decide What to Do Next
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 9. Up to this point, you have already seen how retrieval augmented generation, or rag, can bring external evidence into a language model workflow. You have also worked with language models, tools, vector databases, and validation. Now we are going to connect those pieces and give the workflow more control over what happens next.

[tts-break]

The central idea is simple. Traditional rag usually retrieves once and then generates. Agentic rag can inspect what it retrieved, decide whether the evidence is enough, change the search if needed, call another approved tool, and stop when a clear condition is satisfied.

We will also use a hands-on notebook. It includes a small local Q W E N model, Chroma, Lang Chain tools, Duck Duck Go search, and a custom Lang Graph agent. The core lab can run without a paid language model A P I key.

[tts-break]

As you work through the module, keep one question in mind: does this task genuinely need another decision, or would a simpler fixed workflow be better? That question will help you design stronger projects later.

slides.title: Start with Agentic AI Before Agentic RAG
slides.transcript:
Before we focus on agentic rag, we need a broader idea: agentic A I.

An L L M by itself is not an agent. If I send one prompt to a model and receive one answer, that is simply a model call. Agentic behavior appears when software around the model keeps track of state, chooses among approved actions, observes the result of an action, updates what it knows, and decides what should happen next.

[tts-break]

Think about a travel assistant. A normal model might answer a question from its training data. An agentic system could first check the destination, then search current flight information, then compare options, and then stop when it has enough evidence. The important part is the controlled sequence of decisions.

Our learning order is deliberate. First, understand the agent loop. Then understand tools and state. After that, compare classic rag with agentic rag. Finally, use Lang Chain and Lang Graph to organize the same ideas.

[tts-break]

By the end, you should be able to explain why a workflow is agentic, what belongs in state, when a tool is appropriate, and how to stop a loop safely.

slides.title: What Is Agentic AI?
slides.transcript:
A useful definition of agentic A I is a bounded decision loop.

The system begins with a goal or request. It keeps a visible working state, such as the user question, evidence already collected, the current step number, and any important constraints. It then chooses an approved action. That action might be retrieval, a database lookup, a calculation, a web search, or generation.

[tts-break]

After the action runs, the result becomes an observation. The system updates state and decides again. This cycle can repeat, but it must be bounded. There should always be a success condition, a failure condition, or a human handoff.

For example, imagine a support agent checking a refund. It may retrieve the refund policy, observe that the policy alone is not enough, look up the actual order date, compare that date with the policy, and then stop.

[tts-break]

Notice what makes this agentic. It is not simply using a powerful model. The important behavior is repeated state update and controlled choice of the next action.

slides.title: LLM Call, Workflow, Agent, RAG, and Agentic RAG
slides.transcript:
These terms are often mixed together, so let us separate them.

An L L M call is the simplest case: one input goes to a model and one response comes back.

A workflow is a fixed sequence. For example, extract a value, validate it, and save it. The steps are already known.

[tts-break]

Classic rag is also usually a fixed workflow. We retrieve relevant documents, add them to the prompt, and generate an answer.

An agent is different because the next step can depend on the current state or the result of a previous step. It might decide to call a tool, ask for clarification, generate, or stop.

Agentic rag is a specific kind of agentic workflow where retrieval is inside that decision loop. The system can retrieve, grade the evidence, rewrite the query, try another source, or generate.

[tts-break]

Keeping these architectures separate helps you avoid unnecessary complexity. Do not call every workflow an agent just because an L L M appears somewhere inside it.

slides.title: Why Not Use an Agent for Everything?
slides.transcript:
It is tempting to use an agent for every project, but that usually makes the system harder to build and harder to test.

Use normal software when the next step is already known. If a business rule says a value must be between zero and one hundred, write a normal validation rule. If a user is not authorized to access a record, enforce that in application code. If the workflow is always step one, step two, step three, you may not need an agent at all.

[tts-break]

Use an agent when the next step genuinely depends on what was just observed. Maybe several approved tools could help. Maybe retrieval sometimes fails and needs correction. Maybe the wording is ambiguous enough that semantic judgment is useful.

For example, calculating sales tax is deterministic. A normal function is appropriate. Deciding whether a user question needs a policy document, an order database, or both may require routing.

[tts-break]

A good design principle is this: deterministic decisions should stay deterministic. Use model-driven decisions only where flexible language understanding adds real value.

slides.title: Why Use LangChain?
slides.transcript:
Lang Chain is useful because it gives us common interfaces for many A I application components.

You can absolutely build everything with normal Python. But as a project grows, you may have one model library, another vector database library, a document loader, several tools, and different prompt formats. Without a common interface, you often write adapter code between all of them.

[tts-break]

Lang Chain standardizes many of those connections. A document can be represented with a Document object. A retriever often supports invoke. Tools have names, descriptions, and schemas. Chat models use message objects. This makes it easier to replace one component without redesigning the whole application.

For example, if your controller expects a retriever, you may be able to switch from an in-memory vector store to Chroma without changing the high-level control logic.

[tts-break]

Lang Chain is optional. Learn the architecture first. Use the library because it reduces integration work, not because the project must contain a framework.

slides.title: Why Use LangGraph?
slides.transcript:
Lang Graph solves a different problem. It focuses on orchestration.

Use Lang Graph when state, branches, loops, persistence, or human checkpoints need to be explicit. In a graph, a node performs a step, state carries information between steps, and edges define where execution can go next.

[tts-break]

For example, imagine a retrieval workflow with four nodes: retrieve, grade, rewrite, and generate. If the evidence is good, the grade node routes to generate. If the evidence is weak, it routes to rewrite, and then back to retrieve. That cycle is easy to see and inspect as a graph.

Lang Graph also becomes useful for longer-running systems. You may want to save checkpoints, pause for human approval, resume later, or stream progress to a user interface.

[tts-break]

Lang Chain and Lang Graph often work together. Lang Chain can provide the model, retriever, and tools. Lang Graph can control how those components are connected and when each one runs.

slides.title: How the Module 9 Technology Stack Fits Together
slides.transcript:
This architecture diagram helps separate responsibilities.

At the bottom are the actual capabilities. A local Q W E N model generates language. Chroma stores and retrieves vectors. Duck Duck Go can provide public web search. S Q L or an A P I can return exact structured facts.

[tts-break]

Lang Chain sits above those components as an integration layer. It provides common ways to represent documents, retrievers, tools, prompts, and models.

Lang Graph sits above that as the orchestration layer. It controls shared state and transitions between steps.

Then your actual application sits at the top. That might be a support assistant, a research assistant, a health information workflow, or a class project.

[tts-break]

This separation is useful when debugging. If retrieval is wrong, inspect the retriever. If tool selection is wrong, inspect routing. If the graph loops, inspect state and edges. Do not blame the language model for every failure in the system.

slides.title: Classic RAG vs. Agentic RAG
slides.transcript:
Classic rag and agentic rag can use exactly the same vector database.

The difference is not Chroma versus another database. The difference is control flow.

In classic rag, a question usually triggers retrieval once. The retrieved context is sent to the model, and the model generates an answer.

[tts-break]

In agentic rag, the system can inspect retrieval before generation. If the evidence is weak, it may rewrite the search query. If the question requires an exact database fact, it may call another tool. If the evidence is complete, it can generate immediately.

For example, a classic rag system might retrieve a return policy and answer. An agentic rag system might retrieve the policy, notice that the user's actual delivery date is missing, call an order lookup tool, and then answer.

[tts-break]

So remember: same retrieval technology, different control strategy.

slides.title: What Makes Agentic RAG Agentic?
slides.transcript:
Four ideas make agentic rag easier to understand: state, decision, observation, and boundary.

State is what the application needs to remember between steps. It might include the original question, a refined query, retrieved documents, tool results, a step counter, a draft answer, or a status.

A decision is one allowed next action, such as retrieve, rewrite, call another source, generate, ask the user, or stop.

[tts-break]

An observation is what the previous action returned. That could be three retrieved chunks, one order record, a web result, a validation result, or an error.

A boundary defines what the system is allowed to do. Maximum steps, approved tools, permissions, timeouts, and human approval belong here.

For example, a retriever may return useful policy text, but the grader observes that the order date is missing. The next decision becomes order lookup.

[tts-break]

The important point is that state is not hidden model reasoning. It is the application's visible, inspectable working record.

slides.title: State Is the Working Record of the Workflow
slides.transcript:
State is the working record of the workflow.

Suppose the user asks, can I return order one zero four two? The state might keep the original question. It may also keep a route indicating that we need both policy evidence and order data. After retrieval, the state contains the relevant policy chunks. After the order tool runs, it contains the delivery date. The step counter tells us how many actions have happened.

[tts-break]

Why save these values? Because later steps need them. The final generation step needs the policy and order data. The stopping logic needs the step count. Citation validation needs source identifiers.

A common project mistake is storing everything, including huge prompts and temporary strings. That makes state harder to debug and may make persistence expensive.

[tts-break]

A simple rule is: if another step genuinely needs the value later, state is a reasonable place for it. If the value is only temporary inside one function, keep it local.

slides.title: Observe → Decide → Act → Observe
slides.transcript:
A useful mental model is observe, decide, act, and observe again.

First, observe the current state. What do we already know? What evidence do we have? What is still missing?

Second, decide what should happen next. This decision should usually be small and structured.

Third, perform the action. Call a retriever, database, calculator, web search, or another approved capability.

[tts-break]

Then observe the result and update state. If the goal is satisfied, stop. If not, choose the next action.

For example, after a policy search, the workflow may observe that the return window is fourteen days. But it still does not know when the user's order was delivered. That observation changes the next action from generate to order lookup.

[tts-break]

The application owns the loop. The model may help with a decision, but software must enforce allowed actions, permissions, and maximum steps.

slides.title: Central Example: Refund After 20 Days
slides.transcript:
We will use one example repeatedly so the architecture stays easy to follow.

The user asks: order one zero four two was delivered twenty days ago. Can I still return it and get a refund?

There are two kinds of information here.

First, we need policy knowledge. What is the normal return window? Are there exceptions? That information is likely in unstructured documents and is a good fit for retrieval.

[tts-break]

Second, we need order facts. What was the authoritative delivery date? What is the order status? That information is structured and belongs in a database or A P I lookup.

The final answer depends on both.

[tts-break]

This is a strong agentic example because one source is not enough. It also shows why tool choice should match the type of data rather than using vector search for everything.

slides.title: Classic RAG Trace for the Example
slides.transcript:
A classic rag workflow might retrieve a return policy that says standard returns are accepted within fourteen days of delivery. Then the language model generates an answer from that policy.

That may sound reasonable, but notice what is missing. The workflow may never verify the actual order record.

[tts-break]

If the user says the order was delivered twenty days ago, should we trust that value? In some applications, maybe. In a real support system, the authoritative delivery date should probably come from the order database.

This is a useful lesson for project design. Retrieval can give you relevant general knowledge, but some questions also require exact structured facts.

[tts-break]

A strong system asks not only, did I retrieve relevant text? It also asks, do I have every fact needed to answer this specific case?

slides.title: Agentic RAG Trace for the Same Example
slides.transcript:
Now compare the agentic version.

The workflow first routes the request. It recognizes that we need both policy search and order lookup. It retrieves the return policy, then obtains the order's delivery date from the structured system.

After that, it checks whether the combined evidence is complete.

[tts-break]

If the policy is present and the order record is present, the system can generate a grounded answer. Then it validates citations and any important business constraints before stopping.

This sequence is more reliable because each step has a clear purpose.

[tts-break]

Notice that the language model does not need to do everything. Retrieval finds documents. The database provides exact facts. Normal code can compare dates. The model can focus on interpreting language and composing a clear final answer.

slides.title: Not Every Choice Belongs to the LLM
slides.transcript:
Not every decision should be delegated to a language model.

Some decisions are exact. A step counter is exact. Permission checks are exact. Arithmetic is exact. Date comparisons can usually be handled with normal code.

Other decisions involve meaning. Does this user question ask for policy information, order information, or both? Is a retrieved paragraph actually relevant to the user's intent? These may benefit from semantic methods.

[tts-break]

For example, suppose a user asks, can I send it back? There may be no word return in the question, but a language model or semantic classifier can still understand the intent.

At the same time, if the user is not authorized to view another customer's order, that must not be left to model judgment.

[tts-break]

A good controller is hybrid. Use ordinary software for hard boundaries and exact logic. Use model judgment only for ambiguous language tasks.

slides.title: When Agentic RAG Is Worth the Complexity
slides.transcript:
Agentic rag is worth the extra complexity when the workflow genuinely needs to react to results.

Good examples include multi-source questions, vague user wording, missing evidence, conditional tool use, or situations where the first retrieval often needs correction.

[tts-break]

It is probably unnecessary when one stable knowledge base answers most questions reliably with one retrieval pass. A simple frequently asked questions assistant may work very well with classic rag.

Before adding an agent, ask one design question: does the system need to inspect a result before choosing the next step?

If the answer is no, a fixed pipeline is probably simpler.

[tts-break]

Remember that every extra decision adds latency, cost, testing work, and more possible failure modes. Complexity should solve a real problem.

slides.title: Part 1 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Here is a quick checkpoint.

Which workflow is genuinely agentic?

Option one retrieves once and immediately generates. That is classic rag.

Option two decides which source is needed, retrieves, grades the evidence, may retry or reroute, and then generates. That is agentic because the next action depends on the current state and observations.

Option three simply uses a larger language model. Model size alone does not make the workflow agentic.

[tts-break]

The correct answer is the second workflow.

The important idea is conditional control. The system can change what it does next based on what just happened.

slides.title: Part 2 — State, Decisions, and Stop Conditions
slides.transcript:
Now we move into state, decisions, and stopping conditions.

A reliable agent should feel like a controlled state machine, not an open-ended conversation where the model can keep trying tools forever.

State is the working memory for the current run. Decisions are structured choices among allowed routes. Stop conditions define when the workflow is complete or when it must give up safely.

[tts-break]

These three ideas are connected. Without state, the system does not know what has already happened. Without structured decisions, routing becomes unpredictable. Without stop conditions, the system may loop.

For your own project, try drawing these three boxes before writing code: what do I need to remember, what choices are allowed, and what conditions end the run?

[tts-break]

If you can answer those clearly, the implementation usually becomes much easier.

slides.title: Start with the Smallest Useful State
slides.transcript:
Start with the smallest useful state.

For the first learning build, four fields are enough: the question, retrieved documents, a step count, and the current route.

Do not add a query field until you actually implement query rewriting. Do not add a score until you actually grade evidence. Do not add a draft until a generation step exists.

[tts-break]

This matters because a large state object can hide the workflow. Students sometimes create fifteen fields before the first node works, then spend most of their time moving values around.

A better approach is incremental. Build the simplest loop. When a new node needs a value from an earlier step, add that field.

For example, when you add an evaluator later, then it makes sense to add a critique field and a revision count.

[tts-break]

State should reflect the architecture you actually have, not the architecture you might build someday.

slides.title: Functions Read State and Return Updates
slides.transcript:
Each step should behave like a normal function with a clear contract.

In ordinary Python, you may pass a state dictionary into a function and return the entire updated dictionary. In Lang Graph, nodes commonly return only the fields that changed.

For example, an increment step may simply return a new value for the steps field.

[tts-break]

Why are partial updates useful? Because the graph already owns the current state. A node does not need to reconstruct every field. Smaller updates make node behavior easier to test, and they work better with reducers and persistence.

Imagine a retrieval node. Its job might be to update documents and the step count. It does not need to rewrite the original question or every other field.

[tts-break]

This gives each node a narrow responsibility, which makes debugging much easier.

slides.title: Agent Decisions Should Be Structured
slides.transcript:
Agent decisions should be structured.

If the controller only needs to know the next route, do not ask the model for a long paragraph explaining what it feels like doing.

A weak output might say, I think perhaps we should search the policy because the user seems to be asking about returns. That is difficult for application code to interpret reliably.

[tts-break]

A better result is a small object with a route and, if useful, a short visible reason. For example: route equals policy search; reason equals the question asks about return rules.

This is easier to validate, log, test, and route.

[tts-break]

Also remember that an L L M is not always necessary. If a normal if statement can make the decision correctly, use it. Structured model decisions are most useful when the user's language is ambiguous enough to justify semantic interpretation.

slides.title: Limit Decisions to Allowed Values
slides.transcript:
Once you define possible routes, limit the model to those allowed values.

Suppose the valid routes are policy search, order lookup, policy and order, and answer directly. If the model returns something else, the application should reject it rather than guessing what the model meant.

[tts-break]

In Python, you can validate the returned string against a set. With typed structured output, you can define a literal or enum so the allowed choices are part of the schema.

This converts open-ended model language into a finite state-machine decision.

For example, if the model returns search everything, but that route is not allowed, the controller should not improvise. It should treat the output as invalid.

[tts-break]

Finite choices improve reliability, testability, and security.

slides.title: Stop Conditions Are Part of the Algorithm
slides.transcript:
Stop conditions are part of the algorithm, not an afterthought.

A successful stop might be evidence is sufficient, the answer has been generated, and validation passed.

A safe failure stop might be no approved evidence exists.

A budget stop might be maximum steps reached.

[tts-break]

If a tool fails temporarily, the policy may allow one or two bounded retries. If a high-impact action is requested, the workflow may stop and wait for human approval.

For example, an assistant can explain that a refund appears appropriate, but issuing the refund may require an authorized human or a separate approval rule.

[tts-break]

If you cannot describe how your workflow stops, the workflow is not finished. Every loop needs a reachable exit.

slides.title: Bound the Loop in Plain Python and LangGraph
slides.transcript:
Use two kinds of safeguards for loops.

First, define an application-level limit such as max steps equals three. This is part of your business or workflow policy. For example, allow at most two query rewrites.

Second, use Lang Graph's recursion limit as a runtime safety net.

[tts-break]

These are not the same thing. Max steps expresses what your application considers reasonable. The recursion limit protects you if routing logic accidentally creates a cycle you did not expect.

A healthy workflow should normally stop because its own success or failure conditions are reached. The recursion limit should be the emergency brake, not the main way the agent stops.

[tts-break]

Useful stop reasons include evidence sufficient, answer validated, no approved evidence, user clarification required, or maximum budget reached.

slides.title: Do Not Treat LLM Confidence as Truth
slides.transcript:
Do not treat a model's self-reported confidence as truth.

A language model can say confidence zero point nine six and still be wrong. The number may look precise, but it is not automatically calibrated.

[tts-break]

A better strategy is evaluation. Constrain the decision schema, create labeled examples, and measure how often the route or grade is correct. If you use a threshold, calibrate it on a validation set.

For example, suppose a grader gives relevance scores from zero to one. Do not simply choose zero point eight because it sounds high. Test what happens to real questions above and below different thresholds.

[tts-break]

Confidence should come from measured behavior, not from the model describing how confident it feels.

slides.title: Use Deterministic Rules Before LLM Judgment
slides.transcript:
A strong controller mixes deterministic rules with model-assisted judgment.

Use normal code for order I D extraction, permissions, date comparisons, known categories, and exact thresholds.

Use model judgment for ambiguous intent, semantic classification, evidence interpretation, or flexible language transformation.

[tts-break]

Here is a simple example. A regular expression extracts order number one zero four two from the user's text. Then a semantic classifier decides whether the user wants return eligibility, refund status, or a general policy explanation.

The first task is exact. The second task involves meaning.

[tts-break]

This hybrid approach gives the model work it is good at while keeping hard constraints in software. It also reduces unnecessary model calls.

slides.title: Keep an Action Trace
slides.transcript:
Keep an action trace.

A useful trace records what the system actually did, not hidden private reasoning.

For each step, you can store the action name, validated tool arguments, source identifiers, a short result summary, latency, status, and the next route.

[tts-break]

For example: step two, action policy search, query return deadline, three results, status okay.

This is enough to reproduce behavior and diagnose failures.

Do not log secrets, unnecessary personal data, or huge unfiltered tool payloads. Also, there is no need to store a model's private chain of thought.

[tts-break]

For a student project, a clean action trace is extremely useful during your demo. You can show what tool was called and why the workflow moved to the next step.

slides.title: A Bad Agent Can Repeat the Same Failure
slides.transcript:
A bad agent can repeat the same failure.

Imagine the first search query is refund. The retriever returns weak evidence. The rewrite step produces exactly the same word, refund. The next search returns the same chunks, the grader rejects them again, and the process repeats.

[tts-break]

That is not meaningful reflection. Nothing changed.

A good controller should detect no progress. If the query did not change, change strategy or stop. If the same document I D's keep returning, try another source, filter, or retriever. If useful evidence is always rejected, inspect the grader.

[tts-break]

Every retry should create information gain or change the search strategy. Otherwise, another loop is simply extra cost.

slides.title: Part 2 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Checkpoint question.

Which rule should be enforced directly by application code?

The maximum number of tool steps should definitely be enforced by software. That is a hard safety and budget boundary.

Whether a question is about policy or an order may involve language interpretation and can sometimes use a router.

Whether a paragraph is semantically relevant may use a reranker, classifier, or model grader.

[tts-break]

So the correct answer is: never execute more than the allowed number of tool steps.

Hard limits should not depend on the model deciding to obey them.

slides.title: Part 3 — Retrieval as a Tool
slides.transcript:
Now we treat retrieval as a tool.

From the controller's point of view, retrieval should have a clear input and output contract. The input might be a search query plus optional filters. The output should be evidence objects containing text, scores, and source metadata.

[tts-break]

This makes retrieval explicit and inspectable. It can be logged, tested, graded, and reused.

The important design idea is that the agent does not need to know how the vector database works internally. It only needs a reliable retrieval interface.

[tts-break]

That separation lets you improve or replace the storage layer later without rewriting the rest of the workflow.

slides.title: Retrieval Is Just a Function from the Controller's View
slides.transcript:
From the controller's perspective, retrieval is just a function.

You give it a query and perhaps a top K value. It returns evidence.

Behind that function, you might use Chroma, P G vector, Elasticsearch, or a hosted vector service. The controller should not care.

[tts-break]

This is an example of abstraction. The storage technology is hidden behind a stable contract.

Suppose your first project uses Chroma locally. Later, a company deploys the same workflow with a managed vector database. If the retrieval function still accepts the same inputs and returns the same evidence structure, the graph does not need to change.

[tts-break]

Design the interface first. Keep infrastructure details inside the tool.

slides.title: Keep Retriever Inputs Narrow and Typed
slides.transcript:
Keep retriever inputs narrow and typed.

A search tool might need only three values: the query, a small top K value, and perhaps an approved department filter.

Avoid passing one giant arbitrary dictionary of arguments. That makes validation harder and gives the model too many ways to produce malformed input.

[tts-break]

For example, you might define query as a non-empty string, top K as an integer between one and ten, and department as an optional approved category.

Typed schemas improve reliability because the model knows what fields exist, and the application can reject invalid values before touching the database.

[tts-break]

A small input schema is easier to generate, easier to test, and safer to execute.

slides.title: Return Evidence Objects, Not Bare Strings
slides.transcript:
Return evidence objects, not bare strings.

A good evidence object includes the text, a stable source I D, perhaps a chunk I D, a score, and useful metadata such as an effective date.

[tts-break]

Why keep all of this? Because later steps need it. The grader may need the score. The final answer may need the source I D for citation. Freshness checks may need an effective date. Debugging may need the exact chunk identifier.

If you reduce everything to plain text too early, you lose provenance.

[tts-break]

For project work, think of every retrieved chunk as a small record, not just a sentence. Keep the metadata with the text until final validation is complete.

slides.title: Where Chroma Fits
slides.transcript:
Chroma fits behind the retrieval function.

Module 7 already covered how a vector database stores embeddings and finds similar chunks. Agentic rag does not require you to rebuild that logic.

The agent calls something like search policy. That function sends a query to Chroma and receives the top evidence objects. The evidence goes into state, and the controller decides what to do next.

[tts-break]

This is a useful architecture rule: orchestration should call a tested retriever rather than duplicating vector-database code inside graph nodes.

If you later move from Chroma to another vector store, keep the same retrieval contract.

[tts-break]

The orchestration layer should organize capabilities, not reimplement them.

slides.title: Describe the Retrieval Tool Clearly
slides.transcript:
Tool descriptions matter because the model may use them to decide which tool is appropriate.

A good tool name is specific. Search policies is much clearer than search.

A good description also explains when to use the tool and when not to use it. For example: search approved internal policy documents for return, refund, warranty, shipping, and account rules. Do not use for live order status.

[tts-break]

Compare that with: search for useful information. That description overlaps with almost every search tool and gives the model very little guidance.

Use verb plus object names when possible: search policies, get order, calculate tax, search web.

[tts-break]

Clear names and descriptions improve routing before you change the model or add another agent.

slides.title: Validate Tool Arguments Before Retrieval
slides.transcript:
Tool calls are model-generated application input, so validate them before they reach a database, vector store, A P I, or file system.

Suppose the model asks for a query and top K. First, remove unnecessary whitespace. Make sure the query is not empty. Put a sensible maximum on its length. Convert top K to an integer and make sure it stays inside an allowed range.

[tts-break]

Validation is not only about syntax. Authorization matters too. A perfectly valid order I D may still belong to data the current user is not allowed to access.

For example, a support agent might be allowed to retrieve orders only for the authenticated customer. The model cannot override that boundary.

[tts-break]

Treat model-generated arguments the same way you would treat input coming from an external user: validate type, range, permissions, and allowed scope before execution.

slides.title: Top-k Can Be a Retrieval Policy, Not an Agent Guess
slides.transcript:
Top K controls how many chunks retrieval returns.

It is tempting to let the model choose any number, but this is often unnecessary. A tested application default such as three or four chunks may be more reliable.

[tts-break]

If K is too small, you may miss needed evidence. If it is too large, you may add irrelevant text, increase context size, increase latency, and make grading harder.

The right value should come from evaluation. For some projects, three chunks may work well. For others, you may need five or a reranker.

[tts-break]

If you decide to expose top K to the agent, keep the range narrow. For example, allow values from one to eight instead of allowing fifty or one hundred.

Retrieval parameters are application policy, not automatically something the agent should control.

slides.title: Metadata Filters Can Reduce the Search Space
slides.transcript:
Metadata filters can make retrieval more precise before semantic similarity is even calculated.

Suppose the knowledge base contains policies from several departments. If you already know the user belongs to retail, you can filter to retail documents before searching.

[tts-break]

Good filters come from reliable information: department, document type, current version, tenant, user scope, or another known attribute.

Risky filters come from guesses. If the model incorrectly guesses a department from ambiguous wording, it may silently remove the correct evidence from the search space.

For example, searching refund deadline with a verified retail filter may help. Inventing a filter because the user used a vague word can hurt.

[tts-break]

Use metadata filtering when the metadata is trustworthy and the rule is justified. It is often cheaper and more reliable than another model call.

slides.title: Preserve Provenance Through Every Step
slides.transcript:
Preserve provenance all the way through the workflow.

The retriever should return source identifiers and metadata. The grader should keep them. The prompt can include them. The final answer can cite them. Then a validation step can confirm that every citation maps to evidence that was actually retrieved.

[tts-break]

Useful fields include a stable source I D, chunk I D, source path or U R L, and version or effective date.

For example, if two policy documents disagree, the effective date may tell you which one is current.

[tts-break]

A common mistake is turning rich evidence objects into one large plain string immediately after retrieval. That makes later citation and debugging harder.

Keep the evidence structure as long as possible. Format it into text only when a specific model prompt needs text.

slides.title: Choose Tools from the Information Need
slides.transcript:
Choose tools from the information need, not from the list of integrations you happen to know.

Ask what the workflow is missing.

If the task is exact and deterministic, use normal Python. If you need meaning-based information from internal documents, use retrieval or rag. If you need an exact structured fact, use S Q L or an A P I. If you need current public information, use web search.

[tts-break]

For example, what is our return policy? That is internal document retrieval.

What is order one zero four two's status? That is a structured database lookup.

What is today's exchange rate? That may require a current external source.

How many days are between two dates? That is normal code.

[tts-break]

The best tool is not the most advanced tool. It is the narrowest capability that correctly supplies the missing information or action.

slides.title: Manage Tools as a Small Registry
slides.transcript:
Manage tools as a small registry rather than handing every tool to the model.

For each tool, store useful metadata: what kind of capability it provides, whether it is read-only, a rough cost or latency class, and whether it requires approval.

[tts-break]

Consider three tools. Search knowledge is read-only and low risk. Get order is also read-only, but it accesses structured customer data and needs authorization. Issue refund changes real-world state, so it should be treated very differently and probably require approval.

A registry lets your controller filter which tools are even available for a particular task and user.

[tts-break]

Tool descriptions help the model choose. But permissions, approval, timeouts, and cost limits must be enforced outside the model.

Also log tool name, validated arguments, duration, outcome, and error type. Do not log secrets.

slides.title: Part 3 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Checkpoint question.

What should a retrieval tool return?

The best answer is text chunks together with source identifiers and useful metadata.

Returning only a generated final answer hides the evidence layer. Returning private reasoning is unnecessary and not useful for application control.

[tts-break]

Evidence objects give later steps what they need for grading, citation, validation, and debugging.

So the correct choice is: text chunks with source identifiers and useful metadata.

slides.title: Part 4 — Routing and Query Rewriting
slides.transcript:
Now we separate routing from query rewriting.

Routing answers: where should we look?

Query rewriting answers: what should we search for?

These are related, but they are different decisions.

[tts-break]

Suppose a user asks, can I return order one zero four two? Routing may decide that we need both the policy source and the order database.

Then the policy search query may be rewritten as return eligibility deadline after delivery.

The route selected the evidence source. The rewrite improved the search expression for that source.

[tts-break]

The goal is to use the smallest useful sequence of actions. Do not rewrite, reroute, and call extra tools unless the task actually needs them.

slides.title: Routing Starts from the Information Need
slides.transcript:
Routing should begin with the information need.

Do not ask the router which answer sounds likely. Ask what evidence is required.

If the question is, what is the return deadline, route to policy search.

If the question is, when was order one zero four two delivered, route to order lookup.

If the question is, can order one zero four two still be returned, we need both.

[tts-break]

Some requests need no tool. If the user simply says thank you, the workflow can answer directly.

A router also does not always need one exclusive route. State can record needs policy equals true and needs order equals true.

[tts-break]

For a project, design routes around evidence requirements. That makes the routing decision easier to evaluate because you can label which sources each test question actually needs.

slides.title: Make Router Output Small and Structured
slides.transcript:
Keep router output small and structured.

A router might return three things: a route, a policy search query, and an order I D.

That is enough to execute the next actions.

[tts-break]

The router does not need to write the final answer. It does not need to produce a paragraph of explanation. Its job is to transform a user request into machine-readable execution instructions.

For example, route equals policy and order. Policy query equals return deadline after delivery. Order I D equals one zero four two.

[tts-break]

This separation improves testing. You can evaluate routing without also evaluating answer quality. If the wrong source is selected, you know the router failed before generation even begins.

slides.title: A Plain-Python Router Can Mix Rules and an LLM
slides.transcript:
A practical router can mix deterministic extraction and semantic classification.

Suppose the user's sentence contains an order number. Extract that I D with a regular expression or another reliable parser.

Then separately classify the information need. Does this request need policy information, order information, or both?

[tts-break]

This is better than asking one model call to invent every field when some fields are easy to extract exactly.

For example, order one zero four two can be extracted deterministically. But the sentence, am I still allowed to send this back, may need semantic interpretation to map to return eligibility.

[tts-break]

Use normal code for what is exact. Use model judgment for what is genuinely ambiguous.

slides.title: Multi-Source Routing
slides.transcript:
Multi-source workflows can execute tools sequentially, in parallel, or conditionally.

Use sequential execution when the second tool needs a value from the first. For example, first identify an account, then request that account's history.

Use parallel execution when the tools are independent. Policy search and order lookup may be able to run at the same time.

[tts-break]

Use conditional execution when the second source is only needed if the first is insufficient. For example, search an internal knowledge base first, and use public web search only if the application explicitly permits it and the task really requires current external information.

[tts-break]

A useful project question is: does tool B depend on tool A's output? If not, parallel execution may reduce latency. If yes, keep the dependency explicit.

slides.title: Query Rewriting Repairs Retrieval, Not the User's Goal
slides.transcript:
Query rewriting should improve retrieval without changing the user's goal.

Suppose the user says, can I still send it back?

That wording may be natural for a person, but the knowledge base may use terms such as return eligibility, return deadline, or delivery date. A useful retrieval rewrite could be: standard return eligibility deadline after delivery.

[tts-break]

Notice what we did not do. We did not rewrite the question as, the customer is eligible for a refund. That would invent the answer.

Keep the original user question unchanged in state. Store the refined query separately.

[tts-break]

This separation is important because the refined query is optimized for a tool. The original question is still the source of truth for the final answer.

slides.title: Constrain the Rewrite Task
slides.transcript:
Constrain the rewrite task.

A good rewrite prompt can be very short: rewrite the user question as one concise search query for company policy documents. Preserve the original meaning. Do not answer the question. Do not invent dates or policy details.

[tts-break]

Why be so specific?

Because the rewrite step has one job. It is not a general reasoning step. It should produce better search language.

If you ask the model to explain, summarize, and search all at once, the output becomes harder to validate and may include facts that were never retrieved.

[tts-break]

For your project, define the output shape of each model call as narrowly as possible. A query rewriter should return a query. A router should return a route. A grader should return a grade. This keeps the workflow modular.

slides.title: Do Not Rewrite Before You Know It Is Needed
slides.transcript:
Do not rewrite every query automatically.

Rewriting is a corrective action. First, try the user's original wording. Retrieve evidence and grade it.

If the evidence is already strong, proceed to generation. Rewriting a good query may actually make retrieval worse.

[tts-break]

If evidence is weak, then rewrite and try again.

Before another rewrite, ask three questions. Did the query actually change? Did the retrieved source I D's change? Is the missing fact even available in this source?

If the same query keeps returning the same chunks, another rewrite may not help. Maybe you need a different source.

[tts-break]

Correction should respond to a diagnosed problem. Do not add a loop just because the architecture diagram has one.

slides.title: A Retrieval Grader Answers a Narrow Question
slides.transcript:
A retrieval grader should answer a narrow question about the evidence.

Is the evidence relevant to the user's information need?

Is it sufficient to answer the complete question?

Is the source authoritative for this claim?

Is it current enough?

[tts-break]

The grader should not generate the final answer. Keeping grading separate lets you evaluate retrieval independently from generation.

You can start with a Boolean result, such as relevant or not relevant. But a score or structured result often gives more debugging information.

[tts-break]

For example, a document may be highly relevant but incomplete. If your grader only says false, you may not know whether retrieval failed completely or whether one additional fact is missing.

That distinction becomes very important in agentic rag.

slides.title: Use a Structured Grader Result
slides.transcript:
A structured grader result can directly support routing.

For example, the grader might return: relevant is true, sufficient is false, reason code is missing order date, and next action is order lookup.

[tts-break]

The reason code is especially useful. Instead of a long paragraph, use a controlled label such as missing order date, stale source, wrong department, or no relevant evidence.

Then your controller can map those labels to targeted actions.

For example, missing order date means call the order tool. Stale policy means retrieve the current policy version. No relevant evidence may mean rewrite the query.

[tts-break]

Structured grader output turns evaluation into actionable control information.

slides.title: Relevant Evidence Can Still Be Insufficient
slides.transcript:
Relevant evidence can still be insufficient.

Suppose the policy says returns are allowed within fourteen days. That is highly relevant to the question, can order one zero four two be returned?

But it is not sufficient. We still need the authoritative delivery date.

[tts-break]

This distinction prevents a common rag mistake. A system retrieves text on the right topic and assumes it has everything needed to answer.

Ask two separate questions: does this evidence discuss the correct topic, and does it contain enough facts to support the actual decision?

[tts-break]

For multi-source projects, sufficiency is often more important than simple relevance. The workflow should know when it needs one more tool rather than trying to make the current evidence do more than it can.

slides.title: A Useful Routing Trace Is Short
slides.transcript:
A useful routing trace should be short and factual.

For one run, you might record: route equals policy and order. Policy search returned three chunks. Order lookup says delivered on September twenty ninth. Evidence is sufficient. Next action is generate answer.

[tts-break]

That trace is enough to understand the trajectory.

Good trace fields include the action, validated arguments, source I D's, a score or result summary, latency, errors, and the next route.

Do not store secrets or unnecessary personal information. Do not dump huge raw tool responses into logs. And do not depend on hidden private reasoning.

[tts-break]

A concise trace is valuable for grading student projects too. It lets you show not just the final answer, but how the system got there.

slides.title: Part 4 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Checkpoint question.

The first retrieval returns two highly relevant policy chunks, and together they fully answer the user's question.

What should happen next?

You should proceed to grounded generation.

[tts-break]

Do not rewrite the query just because a rewrite node exists. Do not call every other available tool just because the agent has access to them.

A strong agent does the minimum work needed to reach a reliable result.

[tts-break]

The correct answer is: proceed to generation using the evidence you already have.

slides.title: Part 5 — Grade, Correct, and Stop
slides.transcript:
Now we focus on corrective rag.

The loop has three broad actions: retrieve, judge, and correct.

First, retrieve candidate evidence.

Second, judge whether that evidence is relevant, sufficient, authoritative, and current enough.

Third, correct only if necessary. Correction may mean rewriting the query, selecting another source, applying a filter, asking the user, or stopping safely.

[tts-break]

Retrieval quality is not one simple yes or no property. A source can be relevant but incomplete. It can be complete but outdated. It can be current but not authoritative for the decision.

[tts-break]

Corrective rag becomes useful when we can diagnose the specific retrieval problem and choose an appropriate correction rather than blindly retrying.

slides.title: Corrective RAG in One Picture
slides.transcript:
The first retrieval should be treated as evidence to inspect, not evidence to trust automatically.

If the evidence is good, generate and validate. There is no reason to add another loop.

If the evidence is weak, change the query or retrieval strategy and then grade again.

If the evidence is unavailable, reroute, ask the user, or stop safely.

[tts-break]

For example, imagine a policy search finds no current return policy. The wrong response is to keep asking the model until it invents something. The correct response may be to check an approved alternate source or say that the policy could not be verified.

[tts-break]

The purpose of correction is reliability, not forcing the workflow to eventually produce an answer.

slides.title: Grade Evidence with More Than One Question
slides.transcript:
Grade evidence along several dimensions.

Relevance asks whether the evidence addresses the user's information need.

Sufficiency asks whether there is enough information to answer the complete question.

Authority asks whether the source is approved and trustworthy for this kind of claim.

Freshness asks whether the source is current enough.

[tts-break]

For our return example, a forum post about returns may be relevant, but it is not an authoritative company policy. An old company policy may be authoritative in origin but no longer current. A current return policy may still be insufficient without the order date.

A simple binary grade can be useful when teaching the basic loop. But a structured grade gives more information when debugging.

[tts-break]

The key question is not just, is this document good? It is, good for what decision?

slides.title: Corrective RAG as an Explicit Python Loop
slides.transcript:
This plain Python loop is the heart of corrective rag.

Start with the original question as the query. Retrieve documents. Grade them. If the score is above the tested threshold, stop correcting and move forward.

If the evidence is weak, rewrite the query and try again, but only while the step budget remains.

[tts-break]

Read the logic in plain English: retrieve, grade, generate if good enough, otherwise change something and retrieve again.

The phrase change something matters. A useful retry may change the query, a metadata filter, the source, or the retrieval strategy.

Calling the same retriever with the same query three times is not reflection.

[tts-break]

If one retrieval pass is consistently enough, use classic rag. The loop exists only because retrieval sometimes needs correction.

slides.title: No Answer Can Be the Correct Outcome
slides.transcript:
Sometimes no answer is the correct system outcome.

A reliable workflow should be willing to say that it could not verify something from approved evidence.

For example: I could not verify the return exception from the available policy sources. Please contact support for confirmation.

[tts-break]

That may feel less impressive than producing a detailed answer, but it is more trustworthy.

The success criterion is not that the model always says something substantive. The success criterion is that the system behaves correctly.

[tts-break]

This becomes especially important in projects involving policy, health, finance, or any other domain where unsupported claims can cause harm. A safe no-answer result is a feature, not a failure.

slides.title: Validate the Generated Answer Too
slides.transcript:
Correct retrieval does not guarantee correct generation.

Even if the right evidence is present, the model may misread it, omit part of it, cite the wrong source, or perform an action it is not authorized to perform.

That is why generation should also be validated.

[tts-break]

Grounding validation asks whether factual claims are supported by the evidence.

Citation validation asks whether the cited source I D's actually match supplied evidence.

Format validation checks whether required fields are present.

Business-rule validation checks boundaries that should not depend on the model.

[tts-break]

For example, the model may correctly explain a refund policy but should not automatically issue a refund unless the workflow has explicit authorization for that action.

slides.title: Citation Validation Is a Mapping Problem
slides.transcript:
Citation validation is mostly a mapping problem.

The workflow already knows which source I D's were retrieved. After generation, extract or collect the source I D's that appear in the answer.

Then compare the two sets.

[tts-break]

If the answer cites a source that was never supplied, reject or repair the answer.

This simple check catches an important class of hallucination: invented citations.

Of course, a valid source I D does not prove that the claim is fully supported. A stronger validator can also check whether the cited chunk actually contains evidence for the claim.

[tts-break]

But the first rule is easy and valuable: a citation should never refer to evidence the model did not receive.

slides.title: Evidence Can Conflict
slides.transcript:
Evidence can conflict.

Suppose one policy says the return window is fourteen days, while another says thirty days during a holiday period.

The system should not silently choose the chunk that gives the easiest answer.

[tts-break]

Instead, inspect metadata. Which policy is current? Does the holiday exception apply to the purchase date? Which source has higher authority? Is one document an older version?

This is where provenance and structured metadata become very important.

[tts-break]

Resolve source conflicts before asking the language model to synthesize the final answer whenever possible. The model is better at explaining a resolved policy than deciding which business rule is legally or operationally authoritative.

slides.title: Reranking Can Reduce Agent Work
slides.transcript:
Reranking can sometimes improve retrieval without adding another agent loop.

A vector search might return ten candidates. The relevant chunk is present, but it is ranked seventh. A reranker can reorder those candidates and place the best three at the top.

[tts-break]

That is different from a retrieval failure where the needed evidence was never in the candidate set.

If the correct chunk was retrieved but ranked poorly, reranking is a good tool.

If the correct evidence was never retrieved, you may need query rewriting, another source, a different filter, or a different embedding strategy.

[tts-break]

Diagnose the failure before choosing the correction. Retrieved but ranked poorly and never retrieved are two different problems.

slides.title: Fallback Is a Policy Decision
slides.transcript:
Fallback is a policy decision.

If the preferred source fails, the workflow should not automatically search anywhere it can find.

Fallbacks should be ordered by authority, permission, freshness, and cost.

[tts-break]

For a structured order fact, an internal S Q L system may be the first source. If live external data is required, an approved A P I may be next. Public web search should be used only when the application explicitly allows public evidence for the task.

If no approved source can answer, stop safely.

[tts-break]

Never silently replace an authoritative internal policy source with public web results. Those sources may have different rules, different dates, or may refer to another organization entirely.

slides.title: A Retry Must Change Something
slides.transcript:
A retry must change something.

Attempt one should usually use the user's original wording.

If that fails, attempt two may rewrite the query with clearer vocabulary or more specific terms.

If that still fails, attempt three may change a filter, retrieval strategy, or approved source.

Then stop safely.

[tts-break]

Think of retries as controlled experiments. Each attempt should test a different hypothesis about why the previous retrieval failed.

If the only change is calling the exact same function again with the exact same inputs, you are not learning anything new.

[tts-break]

A good trace should make those differences obvious: original query, rewritten query, alternate source, and final stop reason.

slides.title: Why an Agent Can Loop Forever
slides.transcript:
Why can an agent loop forever?

One common cause is an impossible grader.

Suppose retrieval repeatedly returns useful policy text, but the grader is so strict that it rejects every document. The graph keeps rewriting and retrieving until it reaches the limit.

[tts-break]

Before redesigning the graph, log the current query, returned source I D's, grade, threshold, selected route, and step count.

If useful evidence is always rejected, fix the grading policy.

If the rewrite barely changes the query and the same chunks return, detect no progress and stop or change strategy.

[tts-break]

The graph may be working exactly as written. The problem can be the decision rule inside it.

slides.title: Part 5 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Checkpoint question.

Your agent retrieves useful chunks, but it rewrites the query on every run until the step limit.

What should you inspect first?

Not the size of the vector database. Not model temperature.

Inspect the grader and its threshold.

[tts-break]

If the grader never allows the generate route, the workflow will keep correcting even when evidence is already useful.

The correct answer is: inspect the grader and its threshold before changing the architecture.

slides.title: Part 6 — Build One Complete Agentic RAG Loop in Plain Python
slides.transcript:
Now we build one complete agentic rag loop with plain Python.

This is important because frameworks become much easier once you can see the basic while loop, if statement, function calls, and break condition.

The sequence is straightforward: retrieve evidence, grade it, rewrite only when needed, then generate and stop.

[tts-break]

You should be able to explain every branch without saying, the agent decides somehow.

For example, if the grade passes, we generate. If it fails and budget remains, we rewrite. If the budget is exhausted, we stop safely.

[tts-break]

Use Lang Chain or Lang Graph later when their common interfaces, persistence, streaming, branching, or observability reduce the infrastructure you would otherwise have to write yourself.

slides.title: One Scenario for the Entire Build
slides.transcript:
We will use one question for the entire build.

Order one zero four two was delivered twenty days ago. Can I still return it?

The policy source contains the general return rule. The order source contains the authoritative delivery information.

[tts-break]

That gives each function a clear job.

The retriever finds the policy.

The order tool returns structured facts.

The grader checks whether evidence is sufficient.

The generator combines approved evidence into a final answer.

[tts-break]

Using one scenario throughout a tutorial reduces cognitive load. You can see how the architecture changes without also learning a new problem on every slide.

slides.title: Step 1 — Retrieval Is a Normal Function
slides.transcript:
Step one is retrieval, and retrieval should look like a normal function.

The controller gives the retriever a query. The retriever returns documents. Then we convert those results into evidence objects containing the text and important metadata such as source I D and title.

[tts-break]

The controller should not care whether the implementation uses Chroma, an in-memory vector store, or another approved system.

That means the storage technology can change while the rest of the workflow stays stable.

[tts-break]

The important interface is simple: query goes in, provenance-rich evidence comes out. Keep that contract clean, because grading, citation, and debugging will all depend on it.

slides.title: Step 2 — Keep Structured Facts in a Structured Tool
slides.transcript:
Step two is structured lookup.

A vector database is not the best tool for an exact order record. If you know the order I D, use a direct database or A P I lookup.

For example, the get order function receives an order I D, checks the structured data source, and returns a predictable object such as found true, the order I D, delivery date, and status.

[tts-break]

This is an important project design rule: tool choice should follow the shape of the data.

Use semantic retrieval for unstructured text such as policies, papers, manuals, or notes.

Use S Q L or an A P I for exact structured facts such as account balances, order dates, inventory quantities, or appointment times.

[tts-break]

Do not force every information source into a vector database just because the project includes rag.

slides.title: Step 3 — Route Only When Multiple Sources Are Possible
slides.transcript:
Step three is routing, but only when more than one source is possible.

For teaching, a simple rule can check whether the word order appears and then route to both policy and order data. That makes the idea easy to see.

But do not confuse a teaching rule with a production router.

[tts-break]

A real project might extract order I D's deterministically, then use structured model output only for ambiguous intent.

For example, if the user says, where is my package, the route may be order tracking. If the user says, what are your shipping rules, the route may be policy retrieval.

[tts-break]

Start with the simplest reliable rule. Add semantic routing only when keyword or deterministic logic is not enough.

slides.title: Step 4 — Make Evidence Quality Observable
slides.transcript:
Step four is grading evidence.

The example grader is intentionally simple. It looks for signals related to returns, days, and delivery, and then produces a score.

This is useful for teaching because you can see exactly why the score changes.

[tts-break]

In a real project, you may replace this with a reranker, a classifier, structured L L M output, or domain-specific rules.

The important part is the interface. The controller calls grade documents and receives a predictable result. The internal implementation can improve later.

[tts-break]

Make evidence quality observable. If a grade fails, you should be able to inspect why. A mysterious yes or no result makes debugging much harder.

slides.title: Step 5 — Rewrite the Search Query, Not the User's Intent
slides.transcript:
Step five is query rewriting.

The rewrite should improve search language without changing the user's intent.

For example, a user may ask, can I send it back? A better search query could be return eligibility deadline after delivery refund policy.

[tts-break]

That adds vocabulary that may exist in policy documents, but it does not invent an answer.

A bad rewrite would say, customer qualifies for a refund. That is no longer a search query. It has turned an uncertain question into an unsupported conclusion.

[tts-break]

Keep the original question in state. Store the rewritten query separately. The original question controls the final task; the rewritten query only helps retrieval.

slides.title: Step 6 — Generate Only from Approved Evidence
slides.transcript:
Step six is generation from approved evidence.

The prompt should clearly separate instructions, policy evidence, structured order facts, and the user's question.

This reduces ambiguity.

[tts-break]

For example, tell the model to use only the supplied evidence and to say when the evidence is insufficient. Then provide the policy context with source identifiers. Provide the order record separately. Finally, include the original question.

Why separate these sections?

Because the model can more easily distinguish instructions from evidence and distinguish general policy from customer-specific facts.

[tts-break]

A good prompt does not replace validation, but it creates a cleaner contract for grounded generation.

slides.title: Step 7 — Validate Before Returning
slides.transcript:
Step seven is validation before the answer leaves the workflow.

Check grounding. Are factual claims supported by supplied evidence?

Check citations. Do the source I D's actually exist in the retrieved evidence?

Check format. If the application expects specific fields, are they present?

Check authorization. Did the model recommend an action, or did it try to perform something the workflow did not permit?

[tts-break]

For example, a support assistant may say, based on the policy, this order appears outside the standard return window. That is an informational statement.

Actually issuing a refund is a different capability and may require permission and human approval.

[tts-break]

Generation is not the end. Validation is part of the application.

slides.title: The Complete Plain-Python Controller
slides.transcript:
Now put the pieces together in one plain Python controller.

State begins with the original question, the current search query, an empty document list, a step count of zero, and a route that says retrieve.

The while loop runs only while the step count is below the maximum.

[tts-break]

Each pass retrieves documents and grades them. If the grade reaches the required threshold, the controller changes the route to generate and breaks out of the correction loop.

If the evidence is weak, it rewrites the query and tries again.

If the loop ends without reaching the generate route, the controller returns a safe result such as not enough evidence.

[tts-break]

This is the agentic behavior in its simplest form: state plus a bounded loop plus conditional next-step decisions.

slides.title: Read the Controller as a Trajectory
slides.transcript:
Read the controller as a trajectory, not only as source code.

Step one retrieves with the original query and gets a weak policy match.

Step two grades that evidence at zero point five, below the threshold.

Step three rewrites the query using better policy terms.

[tts-break]

Step four retrieves again and now finds the fourteen-day return rule.

Step five grades the new evidence at one point zero and routes to generation.

Step six returns the answer, evidence, and trace, then stops.

[tts-break]

A trajectory is useful because it lets you explain the run without reading every line of code. For a project demo, showing a short trajectory often communicates the architecture better than showing a giant code cell.

slides.title: Test the Pieces Before the Whole Agent
slides.transcript:
Test the individual pieces before testing the whole agent.

First, test retrieval with a known query. If the expected document is missing, the problem is retrieval or indexing.

Test the grader with evidence you know should pass. If it fails, the problem is the grading rule or threshold.

Test query rewriting. Make sure the rewritten query actually changes when correction is needed.

[tts-break]

Test generation with a fixed evidence set. Check whether the model stays grounded.

Only after those components work should you test the full controller trajectory.

This approach localizes failures.

[tts-break]

If the full agent fails but every component works independently, then the problem is likely orchestration: wrong state updates, wrong route, or wrong stopping logic.

slides.title: Part 6 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Checkpoint question.

What makes the plain Python workflow agentic?

It is not the vector database. A vector database can exist in classic rag.

It is not using the largest possible language model.

The agentic behavior comes from state plus conditional next-step decisions.

[tts-break]

The workflow remembers what has happened, inspects the result, and chooses whether to generate, rewrite, retrieve again, or stop.

So the correct answer is: state plus conditional decisions.

slides.title: Part 7 — Bridge to LangChain, Then Translate the Same Loop into LangGraph
slides.transcript:
Now we bridge from plain Python into Lang Chain and then Lang Graph.

The important idea is translation, not replacement.

A Python dictionary becomes graph state.

A normal function becomes a node.

An if or else decision becomes a conditional edge.

A while loop becomes a cycle between nodes.

A break becomes a transition to end.

[tts-break]

Lang Chain helps standardize models, retrievers, and tools.

Lang Graph gives us an explicit graph representation of the controller.

[tts-break]

If the plain Python version is clear, the framework should feel familiar rather than magical.

slides.title: Why Add a Small LangChain Bridge?
slides.transcript:
Before building the graph, three Lang Chain ideas are useful.

First, the tool decorator turns an ordinary Python function into a documented tool with a name, description, and argument schema.

Second, as retriever gives a vector store a common retrieval interface. The workflow can call retriever dot invoke with a query.

Third, bind tools gives a compatible chat model the schemas of approved tools.

[tts-break]

These are integration features, not a new architecture.

The retrieval function is still a function. The vector database is still a vector database. Binding a tool does not execute it and does not grant permission.

[tts-break]

The application still owns validation, authorization, execution, retries, and side effects. Lang Chain makes components easier to connect; it does not remove application responsibility.

slides.title: Module 9 Environment
slides.transcript:
For the environment, install only what the project actually needs.

If you are studying orchestration only, Lang Chain and Lang Graph may be enough.

If you are running the full Module 9 lab, you also need the integrations for Hugging Face models, Chroma, community tools, sentence transformers, Transformers, Accelerate, Duck Duck Go search, and the Chroma database package.

[tts-break]

Why separate the minimal and full environments?

Because Lang Graph itself does not require a vector database or local language model. Those are capabilities you may plug into the graph.

For a student project, smaller environments are easier to reproduce and debug. Do not install twenty libraries because one tutorial used them.

[tts-break]

Start from your architecture. Then install the integrations that correspond to the tools and models you actually chose.

slides.title: Bridge 1 — Turn Retrieval into a Tool
slides.transcript:
The first bridge is turning retrieval into a model-visible tool.

The tool decorator adds metadata around an ordinary Python function.

The function still receives a query, calls the retriever, and returns results. What changes is that the workflow now has a standard tool description and argument schema that a compatible model can understand.

[tts-break]

The docstring matters. Search the approved return-policy knowledge base is much more informative than simply saying search.

A tool description should tell the model what capability exists and when that capability is appropriate.

[tts-break]

Remember that exposing a tool does not mean the model should always use it. Routing, permissions, and workflow stage still determine whether a tool call is appropriate.

slides.title: Bridge 2 — Build a Small In-Memory Retriever
slides.transcript:
For the first graph, an in-memory vector store keeps the example simple.

We create the vector store from documents and embeddings, then convert it to a retriever with as retriever. We also set top K to three.

[tts-break]

The benefit is conceptual clarity. We can focus on state, nodes, edges, and routing without also teaching database persistence at the same time.

Later, the in-memory store can be replaced by Chroma, P G vector, Redis, or another managed vector database.

[tts-break]

As long as the rest of the workflow sees the same retriever interface, the control logic can remain almost unchanged. This is another example of why stable interfaces are useful.

slides.title: Bridge 3 — Tell the Model Which Tools Exist
slides.transcript:
The next bridge is bind tools.

Binding tools tells the chat model which approved tool schemas exist. The model can then request one of those tools if its integration supports tool calling.

But binding is not permission.

[tts-break]

The application still decides whether a requested tool can run. It validates arguments. It checks the user's authorization. It handles retries and errors. It controls side effects.

For example, a model might request an order lookup. Your code should still verify that the current user is allowed to access that order.

[tts-break]

Think of bind tools as showing the model the menu. The application is still the security guard, the cashier, and the execution engine.

slides.title: Plain Python → LangGraph Translation
slides.transcript:
Now translate familiar Python control flow into Lang Graph.

A Python dictionary becomes typed graph state.

A function becomes a node.

An if or else branch becomes a conditional edge or a command.

A while loop becomes a cycle between nodes.

A break becomes a transition to end.

[tts-break]

This translation is important because Lang Graph is not introducing a completely different programming concept. It is making the control flow explicit and inspectable.

For example, instead of a while loop that calls retrieve, grade, and rewrite, you may have three nodes connected in a cycle.

[tts-break]

If you can point to the matching Python idea, you understand the graph at the right level.

slides.title: Start LangGraph with Four Fields
slides.transcript:
Start the Lang Graph state with only four fields: question, documents, steps, and route.

Those four are enough to demonstrate shared state, retrieval output, step counting, and routing.

[tts-break]

Later, add query when query rewriting exists. Add score when grading exists. Add answer when generation exists. Add trace when observability is needed.

Avoid turning state into a log dump. Large temporary prompts do not need to be persisted. Secrets definitely should not be stored in graph state.

[tts-break]

Minimal state makes the first graph easier to understand. Expand state only when the next node has a real reason to consume the new field.

slides.title: See the Whole Graph Before the Node Bodies
slides.transcript:
Before reading the node implementations, look at the graph shape.

The graph begins at retrieve, then moves to grade.

From grade, there are three possible routes. Good evidence goes to generate. Weak evidence with budget remaining goes to rewrite. A stop condition goes directly to end.

After rewrite, execution returns to retrieve. After generate, execution ends.

[tts-break]

This picture tells you most of the architecture before you read any function body.

That is why I recommend drawing the topology first. It separates workflow design from implementation details.

[tts-break]

Also notice the explicit stop route. A bounded correction loop should have a normal application-level way to stop, not only a recursion-limit error.

slides.title: Node Functions Are Still Ordinary Python
slides.transcript:
Node functions are still ordinary Python.

The retrieve node reads state, retrieves documents, and returns only the fields it changes: the new documents and an increased step count.

The routing function grades the evidence and then applies the correction budget.

[tts-break]

If the score passes the threshold, return generate.

If the score is weak but the maximum step count has been reached, return stop.

Otherwise, return rewrite.

[tts-break]

This is the same policy we wrote in plain Python. Lang Graph has not changed the algorithm. It has made the transitions explicit.

Good evidence generates. Weak evidence corrects only while budget remains. Exhausted budget stops.

slides.title: Assemble the Corrective RAG Graph
slides.transcript:
The assembled graph is a declarative version of the same bounded algorithm.

The normal path is start, retrieve, grade, generate, end.

The corrective path is retrieve, grade, rewrite, then retrieve again.

And there is a safe failure path: grade, stop, end when evidence remains weak and the correction budget is exhausted.

[tts-break]

That safe stop is important. The graph should not force generation from evidence it already judged insufficient.

The advantage of the graph representation is that transitions are easier to inspect and extend.

[tts-break]

Later, you can add persistence, streaming, checkpoints, human approval, or another tool without hiding the control flow inside one large while loop.

slides.title: Debug the Graph with State, Scores, and Hard Limits
slides.transcript:
When a graph behaves badly, debug one layer at a time.

Log the current query, retrieved document I D's, grade or score, selected route, and step count.
