Inspect what each node received and the partial update it returned.

[tts-break]

Then inspect the router. Can every intended route actually be returned? Do the route labels exactly match the graph mapping?

If the graph loops, ask whether each cycle changes state meaningfully. Does the rewritten query change? Do different documents return?

Keep the recursion limit as a hard safety net.

[tts-break]

But do not use the recursion limit as your main stopping policy. A well-designed workflow should reach an explicit generate or stop condition on its own.

slides.title: Part 7 Checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Checkpoint question.

What is the Lang Graph equivalent of a Python statement that says: if the score passes the threshold, generate; otherwise, rewrite?

The answer is a conditional edge.

A vector store handles retrieval. The tool decorator exposes a capability. Neither one represents the branch itself.

[tts-break]

Conditional edges are how graph topology expresses if and else behavior.

So the correct answer is: a conditional edge.

slides.title: Part 8 — Design an Agentic Project Students Can Actually Build
slides.transcript:
The final part of the module is about designing a project students can actually build.

At this point, framework syntax is less important than architecture decisions.

First, choose the simplest architecture that solves the task.

Second, select tools based on specific information or action needs.

Third, add refinement only where another pass can genuinely improve the result.

[tts-break]

A strong project is not the one with the largest number of agents, tools, or model calls.

A strong project can explain why each tool exists, why each state field exists, why a loop is needed, and exactly what condition ends that loop.

[tts-break]

Think of complexity as something you earn by demonstrating a need for it.

slides.title: Start with the Simplest Architecture That Solves the Task
slides.transcript:
Start with the simplest architecture that solves the problem.

If every step is already known, use a fixed Python workflow. It will usually be easier to test, faster to run, and easier to explain.

If the main problem is finding information in documents, classic rag may be enough.

[tts-break]

Use an agent when the next action genuinely depends on runtime observations and several approved tools may be needed.

Use agentic rag when retrieval itself can fail, require grading, need query rewriting, or require evidence from multiple sources.

Use Lang Graph when state, branching, loops, persistence, approval, or resumable execution need to be explicit.

[tts-break]

Do not choose architecture because one framework is fashionable. Choose it because the uncertainty in the workflow requires that level of control.

slides.title: A Practical Tool-Selection Decision Tree
slides.transcript:
This tool-selection decision tree is designed for your own project.

Begin with the question: what capability is missing right now?

If you need a deterministic calculation or rule, use Python.

If you need internal unstructured knowledge, use retrieval or rag.

If you need an exact structured fact, use S Q L or an A P I.

If you need fresh public information, use web search.

[tts-break]

A common bad design is giving the agent three tools called search one, search two, and lookup, when all three appear to do nearly the same thing.

The model then has no clear basis for choosing among them.

[tts-break]

Each tool should represent one distinct capability. If two tools overlap heavily, either clarify their descriptions or reconsider whether both are necessary.

slides.title: Give Every Tool a Narrow Contract
slides.transcript:
Every tool should have a narrow contract.

Start with the name. Use a verb plus an object, such as search policies or get order.

Then write a description that tells the model when to use the tool and when not to use it.

Keep the input schema small and typed.

Return structured results with provenance whenever possible.

[tts-break]

Also classify side effects. Is this tool read-only, or can it change real-world state?

Finally, define policy around the tool: timeout, retry behavior, cost limits, permissions, and approval requirements.

For example, search policy may be read-only and low risk. Send payment or delete record should be treated much more carefully.

[tts-break]

By default, expose the smallest set of tools needed for the current task. A smaller menu usually improves routing and reduces risk.

slides.title: Expose Tools Dynamically Instead of Giving Every Tool Every Time
slides.transcript:
Do not give every tool to the model on every turn.

You can dynamically narrow the tool set based on the task, the user, or the current workflow stage.

For example, every support question may get access to the knowledge-base search tool. If the request references an order, also expose get order. If the user explicitly needs current public information, perhaps expose web search.

[tts-break]

Then apply authorization. Even if a tool is relevant, the user may not be allowed to use it.

You can also change tools by stage. A planning stage might have only read-only tools. An execution stage might expose an action tool only after approval.

[tts-break]

Dynamic tool selection makes the agent's decision easier because it chooses from a relevant subset rather than the entire application toolbox.

slides.title: Refine the Input Before Spending More Reasoning
slides.transcript:
Refine the input before spending more reasoning.

Many weak agent results begin with a poor representation of the original request.

First, normalize. Extract reliable entities such as order I D's, dates, product names, or constraints.

Second, clarify. If a required fact is genuinely missing, ask the user rather than guessing.

Third, rewrite. Create tool-specific wording that improves search or A P I use while preserving the original goal.

[tts-break]

Keep both the original question and the refined query in state.

For example, the user says, can I still send this back? The original question stays unchanged. The refined search query may become standard return eligibility deadline after delivery.

[tts-break]

The refined query serves the tool. The original question still controls what the final answer must address.

slides.title: Add “More Thinking” as Explicit Passes
slides.transcript:
When people say they want the agent to think more, a practical design is to add explicit passes that can be inspected and tested.

Do not depend on hidden chain-of-thought. Instead, create visible intermediate artifacts.

For example: refined query, plan, evidence, draft, critique, and revision count.

[tts-break]

A planning step can identify what evidence is required and which tools may be useful.

A drafting step uses the gathered evidence.

An evaluator checks explicit criteria such as grounding, completeness, citation quality, or required format.

A revision step receives the evaluator feedback and produces a better draft.

[tts-break]

This gives you deliberate multi-step processing without requiring hidden reasoning. It also makes the project easier to debug because every important artifact is visible in state.

slides.title: Reuse One Output as the Next Step's Input
slides.transcript:
Prompt chaining means one step's output becomes another step's input.

Start with the question and create a short plan.

Use that plan to gather evidence.

Use the evidence to create a draft.

Send the draft and evidence to an evaluator.

If the evaluator reports a specific problem, send that critique to a revision step.

[tts-break]

The important design principle is that each step receives only the information it needs.

The tool selector needs the plan.

The generator needs the evidence.

The reviser needs the draft plus concise feedback.

The evaluator needs the question, evidence, and current draft.

[tts-break]

Because these artifacts are explicit, you can test them independently. If the final answer is poor, you can inspect whether the plan, evidence, draft, or critique caused the problem.

slides.title: Evaluator → Optimizer: A Bounded Reflection Pattern
slides.transcript:
The evaluator-optimizer pattern is a useful way to add bounded reflection.

One component creates an output. Another component evaluates it against clear criteria.

The evaluator should return structured feedback.

For example: grounded is true, complete is false, citations are okay, and the missing item is order status.

[tts-break]

The controller then chooses the correction.

If evidence is missing, call the appropriate tool.

If evidence is complete but the wording is weak, revise the answer without retrieving again.

If all criteria pass, stop.

If the maximum revision count is reached, stop safely even if the evaluator is still dissatisfied.

[tts-break]

Reflection should be bounded and targeted. More passes are useful only when they can change the information, evidence, or quality of the output.

slides.title: Agentic RAG Should Correct the Right Layer
slides.transcript:
Agentic rag should correct the layer that actually failed.

If the query is vague, rewrite the query.

If the wrong source was selected, reroute to a different tool.

If the evidence is relevant but incomplete, retrieve another source.

If the evidence is already good but the answer is weak, revise generation without paying for another retrieval pass.

[tts-break]

If a tool fails temporarily, use a bounded retry or approved fallback.

If an authoritative fact simply does not exist in the available sources, stop safely or ask the user.

[tts-break]

This is a very important project principle. Do not repeat the entire workflow because one layer failed. Diagnose the failure and correct only that layer.

More model calls cannot create an authoritative fact that does not exist.

slides.title: A Reusable Blueprint for Student Projects
slides.transcript:
This blueprint brings the project pieces together.

The user sends a goal and constraints.

The controller owns shared state, budgets, routes, and stopping policy.

A planner or router identifies what information is needed and which approved capability can provide it.

A tool gate enforces schemas, permissions, timeouts, and approval requirements.

[tts-break]

Below that are specialized tools: Python functions for deterministic work, web search for fresh public information, S Q L or A P I tools for structured facts, and retrieval for internal documents.

The collected evidence goes to a synthesis or drafting step.

Then an evaluator checks explicit criteria and requests targeted refinement only when necessary.

[tts-break]

Across the whole architecture, keep observability. Record tool names, validated arguments, source I D's, outcomes, latency, errors, and the reason the workflow stopped.

slides.title: Before You Call It an Agent Project
slides.transcript:
Before you call your project an agent project, you should be able to answer a short design checklist.

What is the concrete user goal?

Why does this project need an agent rather than a fixed workflow?

What unique capability does each tool provide?

What information must stay in state?

What can be refined if something fails: the query, evidence, draft, or plan?

[tts-break]

How does the workflow stop? What are the success criteria and hard limits?

How will you evaluate it? Tool choice, retrieval quality, trajectory, and final answer should be considered separately.

Which actions need approval? Anything that writes, deletes, sends, purchases, or approves should receive extra scrutiny.

[tts-break]

Before coding, try to write the goal, architecture, tool list, state fields, and stop conditions on one page. If that design is unclear, adding more agents will not fix it.

slides.title: Build Small, Observe Everything, Add Autonomy Deliberately
slides.transcript:
Let us finish with a practical build order.

First, create one reliable tool and test it independently.

If the project needs document knowledge, build a working classic rag pipeline.

Add a router only when multiple paths really exist.

Add grading only when retrieval can fail in a way that matters.

Add evaluator and revision steps only when clear quality criteria justify another pass.

Add human approval for consequential actions.

[tts-break]

Measure the system as you build. Look at tool accuracy, retrieval hit rate, number of steps, latency, evaluator pass rate, and final answer quality.

You also have companion notebooks for the Module 9 lab, a complete Lang Chain tutorial, and a complete Lang Graph tutorial.

[tts-break]

The final principle is simple: more intelligence should mean better use of state, evidence, tools, feedback, and stopping conditions. It should not simply mean more model calls.

Build small. Observe everything. Add autonomy deliberately.
